title: The last words
tomorrow: and if you wake at 3 a.m. anyway, what then?

lines: I HAND MYSELF OVER TO YOU.
cards: Fall asleep to a podcast, and the last voice of the day belongs to a stranger. A companion of the Prophet named al-Bara' was given another last voice: his own.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told him: when you go to bed, make wudu as you would for prayer, lie down on your right side, and say: O God, I hand myself over to you, I entrust my affairs to you, I lean my back on you.
I believe in your Book which you sent down, and your Prophet whom you sent. Make these the last words you say. Al-Bara' repeated it back to him, and changed one word.
Instead of your Prophet, he said your Messenger.

teach.h: NO: YOUR PROPHET WHOM YOU SENT.
teach.b: The Prophet stopped him. No, he said: your Prophet whom you sent. It's a small correction, and it says a lot.

teach.h: KEPT THE WAY IT WAS TAUGHT.
teach.b: Muslim scholars have offered reasons for it; one reading is simply that words of remembrance are kept the way they were taught, not improved on the spot.

teach.h: SAID LYING ON THE RIGHT SIDE.
teach.b: This is a real Muslim practice: the supplication at bedtime, said lying on the right side, as the last words of the day. And the hadith adds something tender.
If you die that night, the Prophet said, you die on the fitra, the pure, natural state a person is born with.

teach.h: I LEAN MY BACK ON YOU.
teach.b: So sleep is pictured as a small letting go, and the last words are trust: I lean my back on you. That's the shape the whole week has been building.
Read a little, mend what needs mending, set the worry down, put the light out, eat together, close the evening.
Then one line, the same one every night, kept word for word. Not something new to think about. Something to rest on.

how: Muslims learn the Prophet's bedtime practice from this hadith: wudu, lying on the right side, and this supplication as the last words before sleep.

o: a goodbye to say to your family in case of death
a summary of what went well that you say to yourself
one fixed line of trust said as the day's final words

games.q: al-Bara's bedtime words: tap the pairs.
p: washing as for prayer, before bed
how to lie down for the words
I lean my back on you
the one word the Prophet corrected

s: al-Bara' repeated the bedtime words back perfectly
he said 'your Messenger' instead of 'your Prophet', and the Prophet corrected him.
the hadith says to make these the last words before sleep
'make these the last words you say.'
in the hadith, the bedtime words are said lying on the left side
the Prophet told al-Bara' to lie down on his right side.

games.q: your dad falls asleep to the news every night. what does al-Bara's story suggest for the day's last words?
o: a line of trust you choose and keep, said last.
the latest headlines, so he wakes up informed.
whatever comes to mind, so it stays honest.
games.why: the Prophet gave al-Bara' fixed words of trust to be the last of the day, and kept them exact.

practice: Choose your last words: the Prophet's, if you're Muslim, a line from your own tradition, or one plain sentence of trust you could say every night. Say it out loud once, slowly, exactly the way you mean to keep it.
Then let nothing come after it but your breathing.

wordCard.voice: The last words: one fixed line said as the very last thing before sleep, kept word for word, the way al-Bara' was taught.

orig.note: Arabic: the pure, natural state a person is born with.

carryVoice: Your line: the last words, the same ones, every night, word for word. Seven evenings, one week, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 247 (al-Bara' ibn Azib: wudu before bed, lying on the right side, the supplication; 'make them the last words you say'; dying that night on the fitra; 'your Prophet whom you sent', not 'your Messenger')
